scenarios.name: Plants 4 and 5 lost together, shaped like the real TVA and CPLE coal losses of Dec 23–26, 2022 (no storm, no demand surge)
scenarios.summary: Normal demand. From day 5, two plants lose output at once: Plant 4 in the shape of the TVA coal loss and Plant 5 in the shape of the Duke Energy Progress East (CPLE) coal loss in Winter Storm Elliott, with their real timing. At each worst hour the whole plant is offline; for about a day both are down together. After 4 days they return.
scenarios.realData: TVA and Duke Energy Progress East coal net generation, Dec 23–26, 2022 (EIA-930)

source.label: EIA-930 hourly grid data: TVA coal and CPLE coal, Winter Storm Elliott
source.detail: Plant 4: TVA coal net generation, 2022-12-23 to 2022-12-26 (US Central time), below its mean of 2022-12-22 (3.81 GW). The loss peaks at 2.45 GW (64% of that level) at 2022-12-25 11:00 and is scaled so the peak = one whole plant. Only the shape is used: no storm, no demand surge. Plant 5: CPLE coal net generation, 2022-12-23 to 2022-12-26 (US Central time), below its mean of 2022-12-22 (2.50 GW). The loss peaks at 1.24 GW (50% of that level) at 2022-12-24 18:00 and is scaled so the peak = one whole plant. Only the shape is used: no storm, no demand surge.

scenarios.name: Plant 4 loss shaped like the real TVA coal loss of Dec 23–26, 2022 (no storm, no demand surge)
scenarios.summary: Normal demand. From day 5, Plant 4 loses output hour by hour in the same shape as the coal output the Tennessee Valley Authority lost in Winter Storm Elliott, while its demand set a record. At the worst hour the whole plant is offline. After 4 days it returns.
scenarios.realData: TVA coal net generation, Winter Storm Elliott, Dec 23–26, 2022 (EIA-930)

source.label: EIA-930 hourly grid data: Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) coal, Winter Storm Elliott
source.detail: TVA coal net generation, 2022-12-23 to 2022-12-26 (US Central time), below its mean of 2022-12-22 (3.81 GW). The loss peaks at 2.45 GW (64% of that level) at 2022-12-25 11:00 and is scaled so the peak = one whole plant. Only the shape is used: no storm, no demand surge.

scenarios.name: Plant 2 loss shaped like the real ERCOT generation loss of Feb 2021 (no storm, no demand surge)
scenarios.summary: Normal demand. From day 5, Plant 2 loses output hour by hour in the same shape as the net generation ERCOT lost in the rotating outages of Feb 15–18, 2021. At the worst hour the whole plant is offline. After 4 days it returns.

source.label: EIA-930 hourly grid data, ERCOT (2023 calm weeks; Feb 2021 generation loss)
source.detail: Demand: ERCOT hourly demand, 2023, US Central time. 36 of 52 Monday-to-Sunday weeks are calm (no data gaps, mean within 5% and peak within 8% of the season, generation within 5% of demand, no hourly jump over 12%, no federal holiday). Each week is divided by its mean, then averaged: 168 multipliers, mean 1. Plant loss: ERCOT net generation, Feb 15-18, 2021, below its mean of Feb 14 (61.2 GW). The loss peaks at 19.5 GW (2021-02-17 01:00) and is scaled so the peak = one whole plant. No demand surge is applied.

scenarios.name: Plant 6 slow 2-week loss shaped like the real SPP wind decline of Feb 6–19, 2021 (no storm, no demand surge)
scenarios.summary: Normal demand. From day 5, Plant 6 loses output slowly over 14 days, in the same shape as the wind output the Southwest Power Pool lost in the cold spell of Feb 2021 (smoothed over 24 hours). At the worst hour the whole plant is offline. After 2 weeks it returns.
scenarios.realData: Southwest Power Pool wind net generation, Feb 6–19, 2021 (EIA-930)

source.label: EIA-930 hourly grid data: Southwest Power Pool (SWPP) wind, February 2021 cold spell
source.detail: SWPP wind net generation, 2021-02-06 to 2021-02-19 (US Central time), smoothed with a centered 24-hour mean, below its mean of 2021-01-08 to 2021-02-04 (10.66 GW). The loss peaks at 9.34 GW (88% of that level) at 2021-02-17 12:00 and is scaled so the peak = one whole plant. Only the shape is used: no storm, no demand surge.

scenarios.name: Aging plants (4 years of real geothermal decline, played in 120 days)
scenarios.summary: Normal demand. Every plant loses output at the real rate of The Geysers after its peak: about 10% a year. Four real years (34% of output) are played in the 120-day run, so one day here is about 12 real days.
scenarios.realData: The Geysers geothermal output decline, about 10% a year (Foulger et al. 1997)

source.label: The Geysers geothermal field: output decline after the 1987 peak (Foulger et al. 1997)
source.detail: Foulger, Grant, Ross and Julian, Geophysical Research Letters 24(2), 1997, doi:10.1029/96GL03152: production peaked in the late 1980s at about 1,800 MW and then fell by about 10% per year (Barker et al. 1992) because reservoir pressure fell. Here: 1 - 0.9^4 = 34% lost over 4 years, spread evenly over the 120-day run (0.29% of plant health a day). Demand: EIA-930 ERCOT calm weeks.

scenarios.name: Crowding (4 years of real county growth, played in 120 days)
scenarios.summary: Normal plants and demand. Each section grows at the real 2020–2024 rate of its counties. Four real years are played in the 120-day run, so one day here is about 12 real days.
scenarios.realData: US county population growth, 2020–2024 (Census Bureau estimates)

source.label: Real US counties: CDC SVI, HHS emPOWER, Census
source.detail: 3,133 US counties (pop 336,426,684), placed on levels 1-50 by CDC SVI 2022 rank (1 = least vulnerable). Each level is cut into 8 sections of equal population (counties sorted by SVI; a county that crosses a cut is divided). Power-dependent residents: HHS emPOWER. Growth: Census county estimates 2020-2024. The engine rescales each share to its own total population.

scenarios.name: Baseline (real weekly demand)
scenarios.summary: Normal plants. Demand follows the real hourly and weekly cycle of calm ERCOT weeks in 2023. Plants still age, and the Hollow runs close to its limit, so overloaded plants can still trip.
scenarios.realData: ERCOT hourly demand, 36 calm weeks of 2023 (EIA-930)
